article_lead.description: a way to limit the size of fitted weights so a flexible model is less likely to follow noise in its training data

new_bank_questions.title: One weight-decay update
new_bank_questions.body: For one weight w=4, current loss gradient 6, learning rate 0.1 and L2 penalty strength 0.2, calculate the ordinary penalized gradient step. Compare it with the unpenalized step.
new_bank_questions.answer: The penalized gradient is 6+0.2(4)=6.8, so w_new=4-0.1(6.8)=3.32. Equivalently, 0.98(4)-0.1(6)=3.32. Without the penalty the step gives 3.4.

new_bank_questions.title: Feature units and weight penalties
new_bank_questions.body: An input is multiplied by ten and its linear-model weight divided by ten, leaving predictions identical. By what factor does that weight's squared penalty contribution change?
new_bank_questions.answer: It is divided by 100, because (w/10)^2=w^2/100. A raw squared-weight penalty depends on predictor units even when fitted predictions are unchanged.

new_bank_questions.title: Coupled penalty versus separate decay
new_bank_questions.body: Why can adding an L2 penalty to a loss produce a different update from a separate weight-decay step under Adam, although they can coincide for ordinary SGD?
new_bank_questions.answer: An L2 penalty contributes lambda times the weight to the gradient, so Adam's adaptive coordinate scaling also acts on the penalty gradient. A separate decay step scales the weight directly outside the adaptive gradient calculation. Ordinary scalar-step SGD gives the same algebra after matching the coefficients.
